title: You Trust Me So You Can Trust Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article frames trust as a currency that leaders trade in whenever they endorse, refer, or vouch for someone else, effectively saying 'you trust me, so you can trust them.' The author contrasts leaders who are appropriately deliberate about endorsements — treating them as a reflection of personal integrity — with those who either endorse too casually or avoid endorsing altogether out of excessive risk-aversion. The piece argues that this second group misses out on what it calls the gold standard of relational exchange, since reliable endorsements deepen relationships over time while unreliable ones erode a leader's credibility.
points: Leaders operate within a 'chain of trust,' effectively wagering their own credibility every time they endorse or introduce someone to others.
The best leaders are slow to vouch for others, treating an endorsement as a direct reflection of their own personal integrity rather than a casual favor.
Leaders who avoid endorsing others out of excessive caution miss out on trust-trading, which the author calls the gold standard of relational exchange.
Reliable endorsements deepen relationships over time, while unreliable ones erode a leader's credibility and eventually end the reciprocal exchange altogether.
quotes: Trust is not only the most essential building block of relationships and teams, but it is also the currency through which leaders become relationally wealthy.
They place their personal reputation on the line every time they confirm that someone they know can be trusted.
In contrast to others who are quick with a reference or endorsement, the best leaders treat their recommendation to trust a third party as a reflection of their personal integrity and character.
Unbeknownst to these leaders is the fact that promoting and endorsing others is the gold standard of relational exchange. It is the currency that builds, nurtures, and sustains relationships.
If you’re not trading in trust, you’re not deepening your relationships as much as you could. Can we trust you to think about this?
